title: Overloading
description: Several functions sharing one name, told apart by what you pass them.

items: C++ lets several functions share a name, as long as they take different things.
At each call, C++ picks the one whose parameters match the arguments. This is **overloading**.
Without it you would need `greet`, `greetName` and `greetNameTimes`, and have to remember which is which.

steps.note: No arguments. Only one `greet` takes nothing.
So C++ jumps into that one.
A `string` and an `int`. Only the third version matches.
The loop prints the greeting three times.

content.title: Watch C++ pick by the arguments
content.outro: Three separate functions, one name between them.

content.question: Which `greet` runs for `greet("Mia")`?
options: greet()
greet(string name, int times)
greet(string name)
None: it does not compile
content.explain: One `string` argument matches the version with one `string` parameter.

items: A function's **signature** is its name plus its parameter list: how many, what types, in what order.
Two functions may share a name only if their signatures differ: a different number, type or order of parameters (order rarely helps a reader).
Different parameter **names** do not count. Neither does a different **return type**.

items.title: Does not compile
items.code:
int measure(string text)
double measure(string text)
items.text: Same parameters. g++ reports an `ambiguating new declaration` for the second.

items.title: Compiles
items.code:
int half(int n)
double half(double n)
items.text: Different parameter types, so every call matches exactly one.

content.title: Return type alone is not enough
content.caption: At the call `measure("hello")` there would be no way to know which one you meant, so g++ rejects it.

`9` is an int, so it goes to the int version, and whole-number division chops the half off. `9.0` is a double, so it goes to the other. The choice is made when the program **compiles**, from the types in your code, so `half(9)` can never reach the double version.

content.question: Using the two `half` functions above, what does this print?
content.explain: `7` is an int, so the int version runs, and `7 / 2` in whole numbers is 3.

content.value: You Have Used It All Along

content.real: One word, "open", for a door, a jar or a book
content.text: You say "open" and the thing in your hand decides how. `cout <<` works the same way: the value's type picks the version.

content.caption: `cout <<` has a version for an int, a double, a bool, a char, a string and more. The bool version prints `1` unless you switch on `boolalpha`. `to_string` is overloaded the same way, one version per number type.

content.value: You never had to think about which print to use. That is the point of overloading: the library author took the trouble so you did not have to.

items: A common pattern: a short version fills in a value and hands over to the long version, which does the real work.
Only one function holds the logic. Never copy the same loop into both overloads: that is two places to fix every bug.
If the short version only fills in a value, a default (`char symbol = '*'`) is simpler. Overload when the versions take different types or need different steps.

content.caption: The long version is written first, because the short one calls it and must come after it in the file.

items.title: Does not compile
items.text: `call of overloaded 'printBar(int)' is ambiguous`: both match equally well.

items.title: Compiles

content.title: Default or overload, not both
content.caption: **Ambiguous** means it has more than one possible meaning. Pick one approach and the error goes away.

items.title: Same idea
items.text: Both print a score line. One just has an extra detail.

items.title: Different jobs
items.code:
process(total);    // prints a total
process(file);     // deletes a file
items.text: Same name, unrelated behaviour. A cruel trap for the next reader.

content.title: A shared name is a promise

items: Overload only when the functions really do the same job.
Take care with overloads that differ only by `int` and `double`, like `half`. `half(9)` and `half(9.0)` look alike but act differently. Two names may be kinder.

output: Mia: 150 is not a valid score
content.caption: The whole lesson in one program: three calls, two overloads, one place where the work happens, and a bool helper doing the checking.

content.question: Which pair can NOT both be in one program?
options: int area(int s) and int area(int w, int h)
int area(int s) and double area(double s)
int area(int s) and double area(int s)
void show() and void show(string t)
content.explain: Those two have the same parameter list. A different return type alone does not make a different signature.

practice.question: Write two overloads of area: one taking a single side for a square, one taking a width and a height. Call both.
Write maxOf(int a, int b) and then maxOf(int a, int b, int c). The three-number version must call the two-number one rather than repeating its logic.
Fill in the one-argument overload of printRow so that printRow(5) draws five stars, while printRow(5, '#') still works.
This does not compile. Read the error, then fix it by giving one of the functions a different parameter list or a different name.

quiz.question: What is function overloading?
options: Several functions with the same name but different parameter lists
Calling a function too many times
A function that calls itself
quiz.explain: C++ picks the right one from the arguments at the call.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT enough to tell two overloads apart?
options: A different number of parameters
A different return type
Different parameter types
quiz.explain: The signature is the name plus the parameter list. `int measure(string)` and `double measure(string)` clash.

quiz.question: Given `int half(int)` and `double half(double)`, what does `half(9)` give?
options: 4.5, because that is the true answer
It is ambiguous and will not compile
4, because 9 is an int and whole-number division chops the half off
quiz.explain: The type you write decides the overload. `half(9.0)` would give 4.5.

quiz.question: You have `void printBar(int length, char symbol = '*')` and also `void printBar(int length)`. What does `printBar(7);` do?
options: Fails to compile, because the call is ambiguous
Calls the one-parameter version
Calls the two-parameter version
quiz.explain: Both functions could answer that call equally well, so C++ refuses to guess. Use the default or the overload, not both.

quiz.question: When is overloading a bad idea?
options: When there are more than two of them
When the functions do genuinely different jobs, because the shared name lies
When the parameters have different types
quiz.explain: A shared name promises a shared idea. If the behaviour differs, two clear names are kinder to the reader.
